# With an agent


unpatched is built to be used by agents as well as people. The verdicts are
deterministic and carry their evidence, so an agent can pass them on without
guessing. The agent never decides a verdict: it asks.

What is available:

| Piece | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| MCP server (`unpatched mcp`) | Read-only tools: check your stack, ask if a product and version is affected, explain, search the catalog, show database status. |
| Skills | Instructions for four jobs: set up, inventory, plan upgrades, explain. |
| Plugin and extension | Claude Code plugin and Gemini CLI extension that install the skills and the server together. |
| JSON report and schemas | `check --format json`, with `schema/report.schema.json`. Read this, not the text output. |
| `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` | The guide, for a model: <https://amet13.github.io/unpatched/llms.txt> and <https://amet13.github.io/unpatched/llms-full.txt>. |

All of them need the `unpatched` command on the `PATH` (see
[Start with the command line](start-cli.md)), except the Docker form of the
server.

## The MCP server

`unpatched mcp` speaks the Model Context Protocol on stdio (newline-delimited
JSON-RPC). Every tool is read-only: nothing is written, no message is sent, no
issue is opened.

| Tool | Arguments | What it returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `check_stack` | `config_path` (optional) | The report for `unpatched.yml`: findings by urgency with verdict, rules, evidence and `fixed_in`. Packages are looked up in OSV unless the server runs with `--offline`. |
| `is_affected` | `product`, `version`, `cve` (optional), `exposure` (optional) | An answer for one product at one version, without a config file. With `cve` it always gives a verdict (`affected`, `not-affected` or `unknown`) with evidence. |
| `explain` | `id` | A CVE or advisory id (summary, CVSS, affected ranges per source, exploitation signals) or a rule id such as `UNP-KEV`. |
| `search_catalog` | `text` | Catalog product ids by name, vendor or alias, with the version scheme and endoflife slug. |
| `db_status` | none | When the database was built, its age, whether it is stale, and the state of each source. Run this before trusting an answer. |

A tool that fails because of its input (an unknown product, a missing database)
answers with an error that the model can read and fix; it is not a protocol
error. `is_affected` needs an exact version: the instructions tell the agent to
ask you, not to guess.

Options before `mcp` apply to the server: `unpatched --config path/to/unpatched.yml --db path/to/db.sqlite --offline mcp`.

### Claude Code

Install the plugin (skills and server together):

```text
/plugin marketplace add Amet13/unpatched
/plugin install unpatched@unpatched
```

or add only the server:

```sh
claude mcp add unpatched -- unpatched mcp
```

### Gemini CLI

```sh
gemini extensions install https://github.com/Amet13/unpatched
```

The extension (`gemini-extension.json`) starts `unpatched mcp`.

### Any other MCP client

Run the command `unpatched` with the argument `mcp`. For clients that use a JSON
config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "unpatched": {
      "command": "unpatched",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Docker

For clients that start servers with Docker, mount the folder with `unpatched.yml`:

```sh
docker run -i --rm \
  -e UNPATCHED_CACHE_DIR=/work/.cache \
  --mount type=bind,src=/path/to/stack,dst=/work \
  ghcr.io/amet13/unpatched mcp
```

`-i` keeps stdin open, which the protocol needs. See
[Start with Docker](start-docker.md) for the user and cache options.

### The MCP Registry

The server is listed in the MCP Registry as `io.github.Amet13/unpatched`
(`server.json` in the repository), as an OCI package on `ghcr.io/amet13/unpatched`
that runs `mcp` over stdio.

## Skills

The skills are folders with a `SKILL.md` in `skills/`. The plugin and extension
install them. For other agents that read skills, copy the folders into
`.claude/skills/` or `.agents/skills/` in your project.

| Skill | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| `set-up-unpatched` | You want to be told about vulnerabilities in what you run. The agent asks what you run and its versions, finds the catalog ids, writes `unpatched.yml` and the workflow in a private repository, and runs the first check. It does not guess versions and does not put secrets in files. |
| `inventory-from-notes` | You have a pasted list, a `docker-compose.yml`, Kubernetes manifests, package lists or screenshots of admin pages. The agent proposes stack entries (`product` or `purl`), leaves out anything without a real version, and checks them with `unpatched check`. |
| `plan-upgrades` | You have several findings. The agent orders them into a patch plan by bucket and exposure, with target versions from the data. |
| `explain-a-finding` | You ask why something is flagged, what a rule id means, or "am I affected by CVE-X?". The agent answers from the verdict, rules and evidence, and does not turn `unknown` into "not affected". |

Agents should write `unpatched.yml` from facts you give them, never from a guess.
The rule in every skill: never invent a version.

## Evals

`evals/` has small tasks that check whether the skills help an agent: set up a
homelab, read a compose file, answer "am I affected by CVE-2024-21762 with FortiOS
7.2.5?", plan upgrades, explain a finding. Each is scored by running
`unpatched check` on what the agent wrote or by comparing the answer to the sample
database. No results are published yet; running agents costs money, so the owner
runs them by hand. See `evals/README.md` to run them yourself.

## For agents that work on this repository

`AGENTS.md` has the layout and the one command to run before a commit
(`cargo xtask check`). `CONTEXT.md` is the glossary. The end-to-end corpus
(`corpus/`) is the specification: a wrong verdict is fixed by adding a failing
case first. See [Accuracy](accuracy.md).

---

Source: https://amet13.github.io/unpatched/data.html

# Data


unpatched uses only open data that needs no account or API key. A workflow in
this repository builds one SQLite database every day and publishes it. Your Action
or command downloads it and matches your stack locally.

## Sources

| Source | What it gives | How it is read | Terms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [CISA KEV](https://www.cisa.gov/kev) | Known exploited vulnerabilities: date added, due date, ransomware use | One JSON file, daily | Public domain (US government) |
| [NVD](https://nvd.nist.gov) | CPE version ranges and CVSS scores | The yearly JSON 2.0 feeds, which carry a SHA-256 in a `.meta` file; no API key | Public; NVD notice in [NOTICE](https://github.com/Amet13/unpatched/blob/main/NOTICE) |
| [CVE.org](https://www.cve.org) (`cvelistV5`) | Vendor-supplied affected versions from the CVE record, plus CISA's SSVC exploitation and automatable flags (CISA ADP, "Vulnrichment") | A shallow clone of the repository in the build workflow | CVE Terms of Use; the CISA data is CC0 |
| [EPSS](https://www.first.org/epss) | The estimated chance each CVE is exploited in the next 30 days | One daily file | Free, with attribution |
| [endoflife.date](https://endoflife.date) | End of life dates and the newest release of each cycle | The JSON API, once per product | MIT |
| [Exploit-DB](https://www.exploit-db.com) and [Metasploit](https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework) | Whether a public exploit exists | Only the CVE ids from the index and the module metadata | Exploit-DB GPLv2 and Metasploit BSD-3: no exploit code or text is stored |
| [OSV](https://osv.dev) | Package vulnerabilities (Debian, Alpine, PyPI, npm, Go and more) | Queried live at run time, only for `purl` items; not in the database | CC-BY 4.0 |

Attributions and exact terms are in [NOTICE](https://github.com/Amet13/unpatched/blob/main/NOTICE).
The database holds facts and identifiers taken from these sources, not their
prose or code beyond what a finding shows.

Not used: vendor advisories (CSAF) and the EUVD and CIRCL mirrors. They may
come later. Today the fixed version is read from the upper bound of an affected
range, and the newest release in a cycle from endoflife.date.

## How often

| What | When |
| --- | --- |
| The database is built and published | Every day at 02:41 UTC, by `build-db.yml` |
| Your Action runs | As you schedule it; the template uses 06:17 UTC |
| The command line fetches a new database | When the one on disk is more than 20 hours old, or `unpatched db update` |
| The sources are probed for format changes | Every Wednesday (`unpatched db sources-health`), and a failure opens an issue |

The database is published as assets of the rolling pre-release `db` of this
repository: `unpatched-db.sqlite.zst`, `SHA256SUMS` and a GitHub build
attestation. The release is replaced every day, so do not pin to it.

## When a source fails

| What fails | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| CISA KEV or NVD, at build time | No database is built. The previous assets stay as they are, and a watchdog opens an issue. A broken database is never published. |
| EPSS, CVE.org, endoflife.date, Exploit-DB or Metasploit, at build time | The database is built without that source and records it as failed. `unpatched db info` shows its state. Findings still work; signals from that source are missing. |
| The daily build stops for several days | The database gets old. After `stale_warn_days` (3) the report has a "data is out of date" finding. After `stale_fail_days` (7) `check` exits with code 3, unless `--allow-stale`. |
| The download fails when you run | If an older database is on disk, `check` warns and uses it. If there is none, it exits with code 3. |
| OSV is down for a `purl` item | The item cannot be checked; the report says so. Catalog products are not affected. |
| A source changes its format | The weekly health check opens an issue, "Sources need a look". A person updates the parser. Until then the last good database is used. |

The freshness of every source is in the report (`db.sources` in the JSON, and
`unpatched db info`).

## Check what you downloaded

The checksum of the database is verified on download against `SHA256SUMS` from
the same release. You can also verify the build attestation:

```sh
gh attestation verify unpatched-db.sqlite.zst --repo Amet13/unpatched
```

Anyone can build the same kind of file from the sources, and compare:

```sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/CVEProject/cvelistV5 cvelist
unpatched db build --cvelist cvelist --out unpatched-db.sqlite.zst
```

Then pass it with `--db`. `UNPATCHED_DB_URL` points the download somewhere else,
for example an internal mirror.

## What is in the database

Only catalog products go in: their vulnerabilities with the affected ranges each
source gives, all of KEV, EPSS scores, exploit flags, end of life cycles, and a
`meta` table with the schema version, the build time and the state of every
source. Packages are not stored; they go to OSV when you ask. A binary refuses a
database with a schema version it does not know, and asks to be upgraded.

---

Source: https://amet13.github.io/unpatched/accuracy.html

# How accurate is it


**No accuracy has been measured yet, and this page does not claim one.** There is
no published figure for how many affected findings are found or how many
findings are wrong. What exists is a method, described here, and a list of
things that can go wrong. A report with no findings is not a guarantee that
nothing is affected.

## How verdicts are tested

**The corpus is the specification.** `corpus/` holds more than 70 end-to-end cases.
Each one is a small stack, a frozen slice of source data and the exact findings
that must come out (`expect` is exact: a finding that is reported but not listed
fails the case). The cases cover every rule id and every bucket, version
schemes (dotted, semver, calver, Debian, RPM, APK, PEP 440), range boundaries,
sources that agree, conflict or are empty, ignore entries and their expiry,
unknown products and versions, end of life, stale data, and packages. Some use
the shape of real records (FortiOS and CVE-2024-21762, Citrix Bleed, Ivanti
Connect Secure, Nextcloud, PAN-OS).

**A wrong verdict starts as a failing case.** When a report says something is
wrong, the fix is to add a case that shows it, watch it fail, then change the
code. Cases are never loosened, skipped or deleted to get green. This is the rule
in `AGENTS.md`, and a person reviews each case.

**Offline and deterministic.** No test uses the network. Source data is replayed
from `fixtures/`, recorded from the real sources. A case fixes its own clock, so a
run never depends on today's date.

**The catalog is checked against real data.** A wrong name in a catalog entry
would silently mean "no vulnerabilities". A person verifies each entry against a
real CVE record and NVD entry; `cargo xtask catalog verify` re-checks the keys
against the live sources every week; and a product whose names match nothing in
the daily database is reported as unverified, not as clean. See
[Catalog](catalog.md#how-an-entry-is-checked).

**Version comparison is per product scheme, and unparseable means unknown.**
A version that cannot be read in the product's scheme gives `unknown` with the
reason, never a guess or a fall back to another scheme. The dotted, semver,
Debian, RPM, APK and PEP 440 parsers have property tests (the order is total and
transitive, and garbage input never panics).

**No model decides.** Verdicts, buckets and rules are plain code. Every finding
lists the rule ids and the evidence of each source.

## Limits

These are real, and you should know them.

- **Your list is the input.** If a version in `unpatched.yml` is wrong, old, or
  missing, the result is wrong. unpatched does not look at your systems.
- **Only products in the catalog are matched.** Anything else is not checked at
  all (packages with a `purl` go through OSV instead). See [Catalog](catalog.md).
- **New CVEs lag.** NVD often has no version data for a new CVE for days or weeks.
  Such a CVE is `unknown`, and shown only when exploitation signals say it would
  matter. Many of the rest are not shown, by design.
- **Source data can be wrong.** A vendor can write a range too narrow or too wide.
  Sources are combined (one source saying affected is enough), which favours a
  false alarm over a miss. Conflicts are shown.
- **Vendor advisories are not read directly.** The fix version comes from the
  upper bound of a range in CVE.org or NVD. If a vendor ships a fix in a different
  branch, or a workaround without a fix, unpatched may not say so. Read the
  advisory linked in the finding.
- **Appliance version strings are messy.** Builds, patch levels and hotfixes that
  are not part of the version number cannot be compared. Such cases end as
  `unknown`, and can be added to the corpus.
- **A product can be affected through a component** that has its own CVE (a
  library inside an app). That is not found unless you list the component.
- **Configuration matters.** A CVE may apply only if a feature is on. unpatched
  does not know your configuration. It reports "affected" by version and leaves
  the feature to you. Use an `ignore` entry with a reason when the feature is off.
- **End of life comes from endoflife.date.** If the page is wrong or missing, so is
  that finding.
- **The signals are inputs, not truth.** KEV lists what CISA knows is exploited.
  A bug can be exploited and not yet listed. EPSS is a probability.
- **Data can be old.** The database is built daily. If the build stops, you get a
  finding at 3 days and a failure at 7. See [Data](data.md).

## Plans

The repository is set up to measure accuracy: a monthly benchmark against held-out
cases is planned, and so are agent evals (`evals/`). When measured numbers exist
they will be published here, with the method and the date. Until then, if you
find a wrong verdict, please report it:
<https://github.com/Amet13/unpatched/issues/new/choose> (the **Wrong verdict**
template asks for the product, version, CVE, and expected and actual result).

---

Source: https://amet13.github.io/unpatched/privacy.html

# Privacy


unpatched has no server, no account and no telemetry. It does not know who you
are and does not phone home. This page lists every network request it makes.

## What stays with you

- **Your stack.** `unpatched.yml` is read on your machine (or in your own
  GitHub Action) and is never uploaded. Matching runs locally against the
  database.
- **Your findings.** They go only where you send them: your repository's
  issues, and the chat channels you set up.

## What leaves your machine

| Request | When | What is sent | To whom |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Database download | A run with no database, or one older than 20 hours, and `db update` | A plain `GET` for `unpatched-db.sqlite.zst` and `SHA256SUMS` | GitHub (the release of `Amet13/unpatched`). GitHub sees the request like any download: your IP address and a user agent `unpatched/<version>` |
| Binary download | The Action, once per release and runner; the installers | A `GET` for the release archive and its `.sha256` | GitHub |
| Package lookups | Only for `purl` items in your stack, and not with `--offline` | The package name, ecosystem and version, for example `openssl`, `Debian`, `3.0.11-1~deb12u1`. For a package type OSV has no named ecosystem for, the purl without qualifiers. Then a request for each vulnerability id found | OSV (`api.osv.dev`) |
| Issues | In GitHub Actions or with `--github` | The findings, as issues | The GitHub API of your repository |
| Chat messages | Only for channels you turn on | The findings: product, version, CVE, advice | Telegram, Slack, Discord, ntfy (or the server you set) or your webhook |

That is all. Catalog products are matched without any request about them: the
database holds the vulnerabilities of every catalog product, so nobody learns
which ones you run. `--offline` stops the database download and the package
lookups.

The requests carry a user agent `unpatched/<version> (+https://github.com/Amet13/unpatched)`,
nothing that identifies you.

## What you should know

- **Package lookups tell OSV what you run.** If that matters, use catalog products
  instead of `purl` items, or run with `--offline` and no packages.
- **Messages go through third parties.** A chat message about your firewall is
  sent through Telegram, Slack or Discord. Use a channel you trust, or use only
  GitHub issues in a private repository.
- **The status issue and the issues name your items and versions.** In a public
  repository, anyone can read them. Keep the repository private. See
  [the FAQ](faq.md#can-i-use-a-public-repository).
- **Secrets** come from environment variables, are not written to logs or error
  messages, and are never read from `unpatched.yml`.

## The database is public

The database on the `db` release is built from public data and is the same for
everyone. It holds no information about any user. You can build the same file
yourself (`unpatched db build`) and use it with `--db`, so that even the download
is not needed.

---

Source: https://amet13.github.io/unpatched/faq.html

# FAQ


## Why not Dependabot or Renovate?

They keep the dependencies of your code up to date. They do not know about a
FortiGate, a NAS or a Nextcloud server that you installed and did not write. Use
them for code and use unpatched for what you run.

## Why not Trivy, Grype or OSV-Scanner?

Those scan container images, file systems and lock files, and they are the right
tool for that. They find the packages themselves and list every known CVE in
them. unpatched does the opposite: you tell it what runs, at the level of a
product (FortiOS 7.2.5, Nextcloud 29.0.3), and it ranks what matters by
exploitation. The two fit together: scan your images with Trivy, and watch your
firewall, VPN and apps with unpatched. unpatched can also check a single package
you name with a `purl`, but it does not discover packages.

## Why not OpenCVE, Vulners or an NVD alert?

CVE feeds show every CVE for a vendor and leave the sorting to you. About 40% of
CVEs have a CVSS score of 7 or more, so a filter on CVSS is mostly noise.
unpatched compares the CVE's affected versions with the version you run, then
ranks by evidence of exploitation (CISA KEV, SSVC, public exploits, EPSS). The
result is rare, specific and says what to do. It also keeps no accounts and no
server for you to depend on.

## Why is a finding `unknown`?

Because the data cannot say, and unpatched does not guess. Read the rule on the
finding:

- `UNP-UNKNOWN-NO-RANGES`: no source has version data yet. New CVEs often wait days
  or weeks for NVD analysis. The finding goes away, or becomes `affected`, when
  data arrives. Read the advisory and check your version by hand.
- `UNP-UNKNOWN-VERSION`: your version, or a version in the data, cannot be read in
  the product's version scheme. Check the version in `unpatched.yml` (a build
  suffix, a typo, `latest`). If it is right, report it: the product may need a
  better scheme.
- `UNP-UNVERIFIED-PRODUCT`: the catalog's names for the product match nothing in the
  database, so an empty result would not mean you are safe.
- `UNP-STALE-DATA`: the database is old.

An `unknown` is only shown when it would matter if it were confirmed. `unknown`
is never turned into "not affected". See [Findings and rules](findings.md).

## Why does it say my product is not verified?

The catalog ties a product's names in NVD, CVE records and KEV together. A person
checks each entry against real data and records the date as `checked:`. "Not
verified" (rule `UNP-UNVERIFIED-PRODUCT`) means that, in the current database, the
entry's names matched no record at all. Either the product really has no known
vulnerabilities, or a name is wrong. unpatched cannot tell which, so it does not
say you are safe. Report it with the **Wrong verdict** or **Add a product**
template and the entry will be checked. See [Catalog](catalog.md).

## Why is my product not in the catalog?

The catalog is checked by hand, so it grows by request. See
[Ask for a product](catalog.md#ask-for-a-product). For a library or an operating
system package you can use a `purl` today.

## Why did it flag something that does not apply to me?

unpatched matches by version, and it does not know your configuration. A CVE may
need a feature that you have turned off. If you are sure, add an `ignore` entry
with a reason and an `until` date; it comes back when the date passes. See
[the config](config.md#ignore-entries). If the verdict is wrong for everyone,
please report it.

## Why did it not flag a CVE I read about?

Common reasons: the product is not in the catalog; NVD has no version data for it
yet (it may be `unknown` and not shown); your version is outside the affected range;
or the database is older than the news. Run `unpatched explain CVE-...` to see what the
data says, and `unpatched db info` for the age of the data.

## Can I use a public repository?

You can, but you should not. `unpatched.yml` lists your software and versions, and
the issues and the status issue name them. In a public repository anyone can read
that, which is a map for an attacker. Use a private repository. `unpatched init`
reminds you of this.

If you do use a public one, remember that GitHub pauses scheduled workflows there
(see the next question).

## Will the schedule stop?

GitHub disables scheduled workflows after 60 days with no repository activity,
**only in public repositories**. In a private repository the schedule keeps
running. unpatched does not commit to your repository to fake activity: it
needs only `issues: write`. If you run it from a public repository anyway, make a
commit now and then, or run the workflow by hand from the Actions tab when you get
the "workflow disabled" email from GitHub.

## Does it need an API key or an account?

No. Every data source works without one, and the database is public. The only
secrets are optional: tokens for chat channels, kept in GitHub secrets or
environment variables. See [Notifications](notifications.md).

## Does it cost anything?

No. The code is MIT licensed and the data is open. The Action runs on GitHub's
runners and uses a little of your Actions minutes (a private repository on the
free plan has 2,000 a month).

## Does it fix or update anything?

No. It tells you what to do and with which version. You do the upgrade, then
change the version in `unpatched.yml`, and the next run closes the issue.

## Can it find what I run by itself?

Not yet. You write the list, or an agent helps you build it from a compose file or
a pasted list (the `inventory-from-notes` skill). Reading local package lists
(dpkg, apk, rpm, brew, winget, docker) may come later.

## How do I report a wrong verdict?

Open an issue with the **Wrong verdict** template:
<https://github.com/Amet13/unpatched/issues/new/choose>. Give the product, the
version, the CVE, what you expected and what you got, and the output of
`unpatched explain <CVE>`. Each report becomes a failing test case first, then a
fix. See [How accurate is it](accuracy.md).

## Where does the data come from, and is it current?

See [Data](data.md). The database is built daily; `unpatched db info` shows its
age.

---

Source: https://amet13.github.io/unpatched/migrate-from-cvewatch.html

# Coming from CVEWatch


This project used to be CVEWatch, a command-line tool written in Go (versions 1.x
and 2.x). It has been rewritten from scratch in Rust and renamed `unpatched`. The
Go tool is not developed any more. Its releases stay listed on the releases page,
and its last commit is tagged `v2-final`.

The old tool and the new one answer different questions:

- **CVEWatch** searched NVD for CVEs by date, CVSS and product keywords, and could
  watch for new ones. You read a list of CVEs and decided what mattered.
- **unpatched** starts from a list of what you actually run, with versions, and
  tells you only when one of those is affected, with the fixed version, ranked by
  exploitation. You do not read CVE lists.

## What changed

| | CVEWatch (Go, 1.x and 2.x) | unpatched (Rust, 0.x) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Command | `cvewatch` | `unpatched` |
| Config | `~/.cvewatch/config.yaml`: NVD settings, cache, filters, product keywords | `unpatched.yml`: what you run (product, version, exposure) and where to be told |
| Question | "Which new CVEs mention these keywords?" | "Is the version I run affected, and how urgent is it?" |
| Data | NVD API, live, with an optional API key | A daily prebuilt database from CVE.org, NVD, CISA KEV, EPSS, endoflife.date and exploit indexes. No key. |
| Ranking | CVSS score filter | Exploitation first: KEV, SSVC, public exploits, EPSS, internet exposure |
| Run it | On your machine, in watch mode | A daily GitHub Action in a private repository (or the command line, or Docker) |
| Output | Table, JSON, YAML, CSV, text | Text, JSON, Markdown, SARIF; GitHub issues; chat messages |
| Matching | Keyword and CPE patterns | Catalog products with version-aware comparison; packages through OSV |

## Command map

| CVEWatch | unpatched |
| --- | --- |
| `cvewatch init` | `unpatched init` (writes `unpatched.yml`; `--github` adds the workflow) |
| `cvewatch search --min-cvss 7` | `unpatched check` (your stack, ranked by exploitation). To look at one CVE: `unpatched explain CVE-...`. To ask about a product and version: `unpatched check` with a scratch file, or the MCP tool `is_affected`. |
| `cvewatch info CVE-...` | `unpatched explain CVE-...` |
| `cvewatch watch --interval 5m` | The daily Action, or cron with `unpatched check --notify`. There is no watch mode: the database is built daily. |
| `cvewatch health` | `unpatched db info` and `unpatched db sources-health` |
| `--format json\|yaml\|csv\|table` | `unpatched check --format text\|json\|markdown\|sarif` |

There is no equivalent of a free-text search over all CVEs. unpatched is not a CVE
browser; use [NVD](https://nvd.nist.gov) or [cve.org](https://www.cve.org) for
that.

## Move your watch list

Your old `products:` entries were keywords and CPE patterns for products you
wanted to hear about. Turn each into a stack entry with a catalog id and the
version you really run:

1. Run `unpatched search <name>` for each product. If it is not in the
   [catalog](catalog.md), [ask for it](catalog.md#ask-for-a-product).
2. Write the entry with the exact version:

   ```yaml
   version: 1
   stack:
     - product: nextcloud
       version: 29.0.3
       exposure: internet
   ```

3. Follow [Start with GitHub](start-github.md), or run `unpatched check`.

Settings with no equivalent are dropped on purpose: the NVD API key, the cache and
rate limits (the database is prebuilt), and date and CVSS filters.

## Versions and the old releases

unpatched continues the version line: CVEWatch was 2.x, unpatched starts at 3.0.0. Go releases remain
under the 1.x and 2.x numbers and are not updated. If you need the old tool, take
a release from the [releases page](https://github.com/Amet13/unpatched/releases)
or check out the `v2-final` tag. It is not maintained and will not get fixes.

The repository is renamed from `Amet13/CVEWatch` to `Amet13/unpatched` at launch.
GitHub redirects the old address, including clones.
